    Resume Score Checker Workflow: Tailor Your Resume to Any Job in 30 Minutes

    By ATS Score Checker Free Editorial TeamUpdated October 31, 2026 9 min read

    A generic resume tries to fit every job and ends up matching none of them particularly well. Tailoring fixes that, but it can feel like rewriting your whole resume for every application. It does not have to. With a master resume and a resume score checker, you can adapt your application to a specific posting in about 30 minutes. Here is the workflow.

    Before you start: build a master resume

    Your master resume is a longer, private document that holds everything: every role, project, tool, certification and achievement, with several bullet options for each job. You never send it. Instead, you copy from it into a clean, ATS-friendly template (see our formatting rules) for each application.

    Step 1 (5 minutes): Extract keywords from the job description

    Read the posting and highlight three kinds of terms:

    • Hard skills and tools — Excel, Salesforce, Python, Figma, GAAP, Kubernetes.
    • Functional phrases — "stakeholder management", "vendor negotiation", "A/B testing", "month-end close".
    • Qualifications — degree, certifications, years of experience, languages, domain (e.g. "B2B SaaS", "healthcare").

    Pay attention to anything repeated, anything in the job title, and anything listed under "Requirements" rather than "Nice to have". Those are the terms most likely to be searched.

    Step 2 (5 minutes): Map keywords to real experience

    Make a quick two-column list: the keyword on the left, where you have genuinely used it on the right. Be honest. You will end up with three groups:

    GroupExampleAction
    Have it, already on resumeSQLMake sure it appears in a bullet, not just the skills list
    Have it, missing from resume"Vendor management" — you did this but called it "supplier coordination"Use the employer's wording
    Do not have itKubernetesLeave it out; address related experience instead

    Step 3 (10 minutes): Rewrite the summary and top bullets

    You do not need to change everything. Focus on the parts recruiters read first:

    1. Headline/summary: mirror the job title and two or three core requirements. "Financial analyst with 5 years in FP&A, specialising in month-end close, variance analysis and Power BI reporting."
    2. Skills section: reorder so the posting's must-haves come first.
    3. Most recent role: rewrite two or three bullets to show the required skills in action, with results.

    A strong bullet formula

    Action verb + what you did + tool or method + measurable result. Example: "Built a Power BI variance dashboard used by 6 regional managers, cutting monthly reporting time by 40%."

    Step 4 (5 minutes): Check with a resume score checker

    Upload the tailored version to our resume score checker. Look at three things:

    • Does your wording score hold up after your edits? The checker does not read the job description, so compare the posting's key terms with your resume yourself.
    • Is formatting still clean after your edits (no new tables, consistent dates)?
    • Does the optional AI analysis flag skill gaps you could address truthfully, or weak bullets you missed?

    Step 5 (5 minutes): Human read-through

    Read the final version out loud, or ask a friend to skim it for 30 seconds. Software checks structure and terms; people check whether the story makes sense. If a sentence sounds like it was written for a robot, rewrite it for a person. Remember that the goal of passing the ATS is to reach a recruiter — and the recruiter decides whether you get the interview.

    Common tailoring mistakes

    • Keyword stuffing — repeating terms unnaturally or adding a block of keywords at the bottom. It reads badly and many systems weigh context, not count.
    • Claiming skills you lack — it may get you past the filter, but it will surface in interviews or reference checks.
    • Changing job titles — you can add clarity ("Software Engineer (Backend)") but do not invent titles you did not hold.
    • Forgetting the cover letter — if one is requested, align it with the same three or four core requirements.

    Putting it together

    Tailoring is not about gaming software. It is about describing your real experience in the language the employer uses, so both their ATS and their recruiter can see the match quickly. Use the checker to catch what you missed, then trust your judgement. If you are new to ATS scores, start with what your ATS score means and how an ATS checker reads your resume.

    Frequently asked questions

    How many keywords should a resume include?

    There is no magic number. Aim to cover the core requirements in the job posting — usually 8 to 15 key skills or phrases — each used naturally in context at least once.

    Should I tailor my resume for every application?

    For roles you genuinely want, yes. Keep a master resume and spend 20–30 minutes adapting the summary, skills and top bullets for each posting.

    Is it okay to copy phrases from the job description?

    Using the employer's terminology for skills you really have is good practice. Copying whole sentences or claiming skills you lack is not.
